title: A scalable sample-based quantum diagonalization solver for general Pauli-sum Hamiltonians
abstract: A scalable ground-state solver to be used in sample-based quantum diagonalization (SQD) is presented. The solver is built on JAX API, and is intended to be run on GPU platforms and possibly many-GPU high-performance computing facilities. It is capable of subspace diagonalization in up to $2^{30}$-dimensional subspace, with possible upgrades to enable even larger-scale operations. The two main components, a general-purpose eigensolver and an SQD-specific matrix-vector operation function, are described in detail. Efficiency of the eigensolver with respect to the GPU memory is demonstrated using a simple physics model. Furthermore, good strong scaling of the eigensolver in many-GPU environment is observed.
summary: This paper introduces a highly scalable, GPU-accelerated solver for finding the ground state of quantum systems described by Pauli-sum Hamiltonians using Sample-based Quantum Diagonalization (SQD). It details the implementation of a specialized eigensolver and matrix-vector product optimized for massive parallel computing. The work demonstrates strong scaling and successfully validates the method on the transverse-field Ising model.
main_problem: The paper addresses the need for a scalable ground-state solver for Sample-based Quantum Diagonalization (SQD) applied to general Pauli-sum Hamiltonians.
main_result: A scalable solver built on JAX API is presented, capable of subspace diagonalization in very large dimensions and demonstrating good strong scaling on many-GPU HPC facilities.
method: It combines a locally optimal conjugate gradient (LOCG) eigensolver with a specialized, matrix-free matrix-vector operation tailored for Pauli-sum Hamiltonians.
model_or_system: The methodology is tested using the one-dimensional transverse-field Ising model (TFIM) as a physical validation case. The general Hamiltonian is a Pauli-sum: H = sum(c_k P_k).
key_observables: The two lowest energy eigenvalues ($E_0, E_1$) of the TFIM, and the energy gap ($E_1 - E_0$).
important_parameters: Subspace dimension ($N$) up to $2^{30}-1$; the number of parallel GPU nodes (up to 128).
main_assumptions: The matrix-vector operation must perform the projection in situ to avoid storing the full reduced Hamiltonian matrix; the eigensolver relies on the matrix being Hermitian.
figures_summary: Figure 1a shows the energy gap vs. magnetic field for the 30-site TFIM, and Figure 1b shows the time-to-completion scaling with the number of parallel nodes, demonstrating good strong scaling.
paper_structure: The paper first introduces the general problem of SQD for Pauli-sum Hamiltonians. It details the implementation using JAX for the eigensolver (LOCG) and the specialized matrix-vector operation. Validation is performed on the TFIM, demonstrating both the numerical results and the scalability of the implementation.
why_interesting: The development of highly scalable, GPU-optimized, matrix-free solvers is crucial for simulating quantum many-body systems beyond the reach of traditional diagonalization methods, directly impacting research in quantum magnetism and condensed matter theory.
